name: WT1190F
suspected_or_confirmed_origin: Not conclusively confirmed. Leading candidate is the STAR 37FM solid-fuel trans-lunar injection (TLI) motor casing from NASA's 1998 Lunar Prospector mission, based on the object's size and its very low bulk density; no spectroscopic or documentary proof of identity was obtained before it burned up, so the identification remains a strong inference rather than a certainty.
discovery: First imaged, unrecognized, by the Mount Lemmon Survey on 2009-10-26 (9U01FF6); briefly re-observed and lost twice more (2013-02-18 as UDA34A3, observed 5 hours; 2013-11-29 as UW8551D, observed 1h35m) before Catalina Sky Survey observer Rose Garcia linked these detections and designated it WT1190F on 2015-10-03, roughly six weeks before it reentered.
orbital_history: Highly eccentric, Earth-bound geocentric orbit (2015 epoch): periapsis 21,222 km, apoapsis 655,374 km (1.70 lunar distances), eccentricity 0.937, period 22.66 days, inclination 3.2 deg. Unlike the temporarily-captured objects below, WT1190F was already gravitationally bound to Earth in a stable-looking orbit for years before its orbit finally decayed into the atmosphere.
identification_evidence: Bulk density of only about 0.10 g/cm^3 and strong sensitivity to solar radiation pressure (a large area-to-mass ratio) are incompatible with a solid natural rock and consistent with a lightweight hollow shell such as a spent rocket motor casing or propellant tank.
physical_characteristics: 0.7-2 m across, estimated mass 250-2,000 kg, tumbling with a rotation period of about 0.75 s; apparent magnitude ranged 16-23 as it approached.
outcome: Reentered exactly as predicted at 06:18:21.7 UTC on 2015-11-13, about 100 km off Galle, Sri Lanka, at roughly 11 km/s. Produced a bright daytime fireball; almost all material was destroyed or fell into the Indian Ocean and nothing was recovered.
scientific_significance: The first-ever precisely predicted reentry of a piece of space debris. Because the trajectory was public and accurate to well under a second, ESA and the UAE Space Agency chartered a Gulfstream 450 jet — with SETI Institute's Peter Jenniskens aboard — to fly above the cloud deck and film the reentry and its spectrum, deliberately using WT1190F as a rehearsal for how a short-warning natural asteroid impact would be tracked, predicted, and observed (Jenniskens et al. 2016; Micheli et al. 2018).
comparison_to_neo_impactor_set: WT1190F is the closest artificial analog to the 13 natural impactors: discovered weeks ahead, its reentry time was called to a tenth of a second (matching 2024 RW1's precision), and ESA/researchers explicitly used it as a proxy for natural-impactor response planning. The key difference is starting condition — WT1190F had already been a quiet Earth satellite for years, while all 13 natural cases arrived fresh from interplanetary space on their first (and only) close approach. No natural case in the 13-object set has ever had its progenitor traced to a specific known piece of hardware, however tentatively; WT1190F's low density did that work for free.

key_papers.topic: Airborne observations of an asteroid entry for high fidelity modeling: space debris object WT1190F

key_papers.authors: Micheli, M., Buzzoni, A., Koschny, D., Drolshagen, G., Perozzi, E., Hainaut, O., Lemmens, S., et al.
key_papers.topic: The observing campaign on the deep-space debris WT1190F as a test case for short-warning NEO impacts

name: 2020 SO
suspected_or_confirmed_origin: Confirmed: the Centaur upper stage that launched NASA's Surveyor 2 lander toward the Moon on 1966-09-20. Surveyor 2 itself crashed on the Moon; its spent Centaur stage missed the Moon and drifted into a wide, Earth-like heliocentric orbit for 54 years.
discovery: Discovered 2020-09-17 by the Pan-STARRS1 survey at Haleakala Observatory (provisional designation P116rK2); its orbit was quickly noted as unusually Earth-like.
orbital_history: Pre-capture (2020 May): a=1.0371 AU, e=0.034, Apollo-class, Earth MOID 0.0163 AU. Entered Earth's Hill sphere 2020-11-08 and became temporarily gravitationally bound; closest approach 2020-12-01 (~50,000 km from Earth's center, outside the geostationary belt); a second, more distant approach 2021-02-02 (~220,000 km). During capture (Dec 2020): a=0.9865 AU, e=0.0018, reclassified as an Atira orbit. Departed the Hill sphere around 2021-03-08, returning to independent heliocentric orbit. Removed from the Minor Planet Center's minor-planet database on 2021-02-19 once its artificial nature was confirmed.
identification_evidence: December 2020 spectroscopy with NASA's Infrared Telescope Facility (IRTF) found a reflectance spectrum matching stainless steel rather than any known asteroid taxonomic class; radar and photometric rotation period (~9.4-9.5 s) and a 2.5-magnitude light-curve amplitude indicated an elongated, tumbling artificial body (~10 m x 3 m) rather than a compact rock; the orbital-dynamics match to a Surveyor 2 Centaur departure in September 1966 was independently confirmed to within days by JPL's Center for Near-Earth Object Studies.
physical_characteristics: Elongated cylindrical shape roughly 10 m long by 3 m wide, consistent with an Atlas-Centaur upper stage; strongly affected by solar radiation pressure given its large area-to-mass ratio.
outcome: Did not reenter. After roughly four months as a temporarily captured 'minimoon,' it escaped Earth's gravity again in March 2021 and resumed an independent heliocentric orbit.
scientific_significance: The clearest spectroscopically confirmed identification of a specific 1960s-era rocket stage rediscovered in deep space; established stainless-steel reflectance and slow multi-second rotation as diagnostic signatures for other candidate objects, and demonstrated that JPL's orbit-propagation models can trace a decades-old departure trajectory back to a specific known launch to within days.
comparison_to_neo_impactor_set: 2020 SO shows why a confirmed Earth reentry of deep-space hardware (WT1190F) is rare rather than routine: an object can be captured, closely approach Earth well inside the Moon's distance, and still escape again rather than decay into the atmosphere, because these lightweight, high-area-to-mass-ratio objects are pushed around by solar radiation pressure in ways compact natural asteroids are not. None of the 13 natural impactors show this back-and-forth capture behavior — they each made one hyperbolic approach and struck.

key_papers.authors: Center for Near-Earth Object Studies (JPL), Ye, Q., et al.
key_papers.journal_or_venue: NASA/JPL public technical statements and IAU Minor Planet Electronic Circulars
key_papers.topic: Orbital identification of 2020 SO as the Surveyor 2 Centaur upper stage

name: J002E3
date_utc: 1969-11-18 (captured after lunar flyby) to 2003-06 (escaped to heliocentric orbit); 2002-09-03 (rediscovered)
suspected_or_confirmed_origin: Confirmed via spectroscopy: the S-IVB third stage of the Apollo 12 Saturn V rocket.
discovery: Rediscovered 2002-09-03 by amateur astronomer Bill Yeung, who initially reported it as a possible new asteroid; professional follow-up quickly flagged its Earth-like orbit and slow, deliberate tumble as anomalous for a natural body.
orbital_history: NASA intended to vent the Apollo 12 S-IVB's residual propellant to send it into permanent heliocentric orbit after translunar injection, but an unusually long ullage-motor burn left it without enough energy to fully escape the Earth-Moon system; instead it entered a loosely bound, chaotic high-Earth orbit after a lunar flyby on 1969-11-18. It left Earth's vicinity in 1971, was rediscovered as J002E3 in Earth orbit in 2002, and departed again into heliocentric orbit around June 2003. Its geocentric/heliocentric cycling recurs on a roughly 40-year period, with a return to Earth's vicinity anticipated in the mid-2040s.
identification_evidence: University of Arizona spectroscopy found absorption features matching white paint, black paint, and aluminum consistent with Saturn V hardware, with a titanium-dioxide-pigment signature specifically pointing to Apollo-era rocket paint rather than any mineral surface. Its very slow 63.46 s end-over-end tumble (with 79 deg +/- 10 deg precession) is also inconsistent with a compact asteroid and consistent with a large, low-density hollow stage.
physical_characteristics: Full S-IVB stage, roughly 14 tonnes; large hollow structure with a correspondingly large area-to-mass ratio, making it highly susceptible to solar radiation pressure perturbation.
outcome: Did not reenter. Left Earth orbit again in 2003 for an independent heliocentric orbit; not expected back near Earth until roughly the 2040s.
scientific_significance: The first deep-space human-made object to be rediscovered, spectroscopically confirmed, and traced to a specific historical mission (Chodas & Chesley 2002; Jorgensen et al. 2003), establishing the paint-spectroscopy technique later applied to other rediscovered stages and giving orbital dynamicists a real, decades-long case study in Earth-Moon-Sun three-body capture and escape for artificial bodies.
comparison_to_neo_impactor_set: J002E3 is the longest-baseline example of the same population WT1190F came from: Saturn V third stages deliberately sent toward solar orbit that instead lingered near Earth for decades. Its ~40-year capture/escape cycle underscores that most such derelict deep-space hardware does not simply come home — it oscillates near Earth indefinitely, unlike any of the 13 natural impactors, each of which was on its one and only Earth-crossing approach when detected.

key_papers.authors: Chodas, P. W., Chesley, S. R.
key_papers.topic: Orbital analysis identifying J002E3 as a candidate Apollo 12 S-IVB stage

name: WE0913A (Chang'e 5-T1 booster / Long March 3C third stage)
suspected_or_confirmed_origin: Confirmed via spectral and trajectory analysis: the Long March 3C third stage that launched China's Chang'e 5-T1 lunar-return test mission on 2014-10-23.
origin_space_program: CNSA (China National Space Administration), Chang'e program
discovery: Tracked as unidentified deep-space debris for over seven years after the 2014 launch; in early 2022, orbital projections showed it was on course to strike the Moon, triggering a public identification dispute — it was initially misattributed to the second stage of the SpaceX Falcon 9 that launched NASA's DSCOVR mission in 2015.
orbital_history: Left in a trans-lunar trajectory after the 2014 Chang'e 5-T1 launch rather than being sent to a stable disposal orbit; made repeated close flybys of the Earth and Moon over the following years before impacting the lunar far side.
identification_evidence: University of Arizona ground-based spectroscopy and trajectory back-propagation confirmed the Chinese origin and ruled out the Falcon 9 second stage; the US Space Command separately confirmed the object never reentered Earth's atmosphere, contradicting an initial Chinese foreign-ministry denial of ownership.
physical_characteristics: A double impact crater roughly 29 m wide was later imaged by NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter and India's Chandrayaan-2, an unusual morphology researchers attribute to an unknown second mass attached to the stage at impact.
outcome: Impacted the Moon's far side near Hertzsprung crater (5.18N, 233.55E) on 2022-03-04 at several km/s; this is a lunar impact, not an Earth reentry, and is included here only for contrast.
scientific_significance: Demonstrated, seven years after the fact, how easily derelict trans-lunar-injection hardware from different national programs can be confused with one another when no one deliberately tracks it; the eventual identification relied on the same spectroscopic and dynamical toolkit used for WT1190F, 2020 SO, and J002E3.
comparison_to_neo_impactor_set: Not an Earth-reentry case, but it demonstrates the broader population these Earth-reentry candidates are drawn from: multiple national programs (US and Chinese here) have left translunar-injection stages drifting for years to decades, and only careful, deliberate tracking — the same infrastructure built for natural NEOs — can tell whose derelict hardware is about to hit something, and what.

key_papers.authors: University of Arizona / Planetary Science Institute team
key_papers.topic: Physical characterization of Moon impactor WE0913A

name: 1991 VG
suspected_or_confirmed_origin: Resolved as natural. No compelling evidence was ever found for an artificial origin despite early speculation.
origin_space_program: None — considered by some in 1991-1992 to possibly be Apollo-program or other 1960s-70s launch debris, but never linked to any specific mission.
discovery: Discovered 1991-11-06 by James Scotti using the Spacewatch telescope at Kitt Peak; its unusually Earth-like orbit (semi-major axis 1.03 AU, low eccentricity, Earth MOID ~0.002 AU) drew immediate attention as one of the most Earth-similar orbits then known for a small object.
orbital_history: Semi-major axis 1.0323 AU, eccentricity 0.052, orbital period 383 days — essentially co-orbital with Earth. Made a close approach of 0.003 AU (450,000 km) on 1991-12-05, and later returned for closer study on 2017-08-07 (0.057 AU) and 2018-02-11 (0.047 AU).
identification_evidence: Rapid brightness variation seen near its 1991 close approach fueled speculation about a tumbling artificial object (a spent rocket tank or Apollo-era debris), but later analysis found no photometric, spectroscopic, or dynamical evidence inconsistent with a natural small asteroid; the working scientific conclusion is that 1991 VG is natural, though its unusual orbit (possibly lunar-ejecta-related, like 2024 PT5) remains of independent interest.
physical_characteristics: Roughly 5-12 m across, in the same size range as several of the 13 tracked natural impactors and the smaller deep-space artificial candidates.
outcome: No impact or capture; a natural close approach, now resolved as such, with no further anomaly.
scientific_significance: An early (pre-WT1190F, pre-2020 SO) case study in how hard it is to tell a natural Earth-co-orbital object from artificial debris using early-1990s instrumentation, and a caution against over-reading brightness variability alone as evidence of artificiality.
comparison_to_neo_impactor_set: 1991 VG is the mirror image of WT1190F/2020 SO/J002E3: a case where the artificial-origin hypothesis was reasonable to raise but did not survive scrutiny, just as 2024 PT5 (lunar ejecta) was later confirmed natural using the same area-to-mass-ratio radiation-pressure test that helped confirm WT1190F's and 2020 SO's artificial nature. Included to show the identification methodology cuts both ways, and is not a foregone conclusion in either direction.
